zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical reference consulted: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; licensed CC BY 4.0: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Diplomatic readings are based on the supplied BnF scan; corrections and English review notes are this reviewer’s work, not a transcription supplied by NINJAL.

lines.note: Continues the preceding explanation with “different directions”; me ga gurimeku then introduces restless movement of the eyes. The Portuguese verb begins with Bu- and continues on the next row.

runs.text: lirem, ou pestenejarem muito os olhos, como

lines.note: Completes Bulirem and adds frequent blinking. The printed pestenejarem is retained rather than replaced with a modern spelling of the verb.
The comparison is with an eye containing a speck or foreign body (argueiro). This closes the example introduced by Mega gurimequ.
Me is the female or wife sense, distinct from the eye-related homographs around it. The Portuguese explicitly includes a married woman.
This separate me denotes a kind of marine weed, described as sea limos. No modern botanical species is supplied.
Me here means points or graduation marks; enlargement restores the i in riſcas. Facarimeuo xi- starts the example about recognizing the marks of a weighing instrument.

runs.text: Não ſaber os pontos do Dachem.

lines.note: Ranu completes shiranu: not knowing or understanding the scale divisions. Dachem is the instrument-name embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not part of the Japanese example.
Me ga kiyeta means that the marks have disappeared. The divided Portuguese riſ- belongs with cas on the next row.
Cas completes riſcas; the gloss says that the strokes or points are no longer visible, continuing Mega qiyeta.

runs.text: He particula que posta com as raizes dal-

lines.note: This me is a suffix added to verb stems. The explanation begins here and describes a boundary or result of the action rather than a free-standing noun.

runs.text: gũs verbos ſignifica o termo da acção dos taes

lines.note: The suffix denotes the endpoint or resulting mark of the verbs concerned. The scan supports ſignifica, not the provisional ſignifira.
Kirime illustrates the suffix as a wound or cut-mark. Vt belongs to the italic explanatory apparatus; Qirime remains roman.
Kawarime is a juncture or the start of a change. Its definition continues on a physical row omitted by the provisional OCR, now restored as c1-l013a.
Completes the definition of kawarime and introduces yo no kawarime ni, at a change of age or time. This entire physical row was missing from the draft; the final Na begins its Portuguese translation.
Completes the restored example: at a change of age or time. The print reads mudança da idade, without the provisional nasal mark on idade; Nui- starts nuime.

runs.text: Sinal das linhas com que ſe coſe, ou

lines.note: Me completes nuime, the marks or seams made by sewing thread. The Portuguese coſe is the sewing verb, not a cooking term.
Custura closes the sewing definition as an alternative to coſe. The historical spelling with initial cu- is preserved.

runs.text: He particula que abaixa os nomes com que

lines.note: This suffix me disparages the noun to which it is attached. It is a separate grammatical use from the action-result suffix above.
Ano yatsume is the contemptuous “that fellow.” The Portuguese Aquelle begins its translation, with the depreciatory noun on the next row.
Madraço supplies the derogatory characterization of that fellow. This is the close of the suffix example, not a separate entry.

runs.text: Aluo, ou ſinal qualquer a que ſe tira cõ

lines.note: Meate is a target or mark aimed at. The Portuguese instrumental phrase starts with the abbreviated cõ and continues with bow or firearm.

runs.text: arco, ou eſpingarda. ¶ Item, per met.

lines.note: A bow and an espingarda supply the literal shooting context. Item, per met. then introduces a transferred meaning of meate.

runs.text: Aluo, ou regra polla qual ſe hum regula. Vt,

lines.note: The figurative target is a rule or standard by which someone guides himself. The visibly italic Vt introduces the Japanese example below.
Ano hito wo meate ni shite mooshita means speaking with that person as the reference or intended target. The translation here emphasizes taking him as one’s standard.

runs.text: tomando aquelle homẽ por regra, ou methodo.

lines.note: Completes the translation: taking that man as a rule or method. The scan reads homẽ; the provisional homtẽ inserted a consonant not present in the print.
Meate ga chigoota means missing the target. Enlargement shows t in Meatega, correcting the provisional Mearega; the caron in chigǒta is retained.

runs.text: ¶ Item, per met. Errou no que cuidaua, ou

lines.note: The same expression is extended metaphorically to being mistaken in one’s supposition. The object of that mistaken judgment continues below.
Completes the figurative explanation with what one had seen and perceived. Focutouo begins the next Japanese example, concerning a northern celestial guide.
Hokuto wo meate ni shite fune wo noru describes navigating with Hokuto as one’s guide. The Portuguese translation starts Nauegar tomã- and continues on the following row.

runs.text: do a estrella do norte por guia, & regra.

lines.note: Completes tomando and identifies the guide as the north star. The gloss’s description is retained without silently equating the Japanese celestial name with a modern astronomical identification.

runs.text: Peſſoa que alcança bem com a vi-

lines.note: Mebayana describes someone quick or keen of sight. The printed final na belongs to the adjectival form rather than being an erroneous extra syllable.

runs.text: ſta, ou enxerga logo com os olhos algũa couſa

lines.note: Completes viſta and explains immediately noticing something with the eyes. The tilde belongs to u in algũa; the faint mark after couſa is not promoted to secure punctuation.

runs.text: Inſtrumento de metal pera por mezi-

lines.note: Mebǒ is a metal instrument for applying eye medicine. The visibly downward mark over o is retained as a caron, and mezi- continues as mezinhas below.
Nhas completes mezinhas: medicines put into the eyes with the preceding metal applicator. The short row belongs entirely to Mebǒ.
Meboshi denotes the lights or “stars” perceived in the eyes. The Portuguese explains them in terms of vital spirits and begins the diminutive lumeſi- across the line break.

runs.text: nhos ſe a leuantão às vezes nos olhos. ¶

lines.note: Nhos completes the comparison with little lights arising in the eyes. Me- begins the illustrative phrase on the next row; the wording belongs to the source’s explanation, not a modern physiological assertion.
Meboshi no hana ga chiru describes these eye-lights scattering. The Portuguese Aleuantaremſe starts its explanation and continues eſ- as eſtes below.

runs.text: tes eſpiritus vitaes dentro nos olhos.

lines.note: Completes eſtes and places the vital spirits within the eyes. The final B. is an upright register label, outside the italic gloss.
Mekake is a mistress or concubine, directly glossed manceba. The historical word is retained without broadening it to an ordinary wife.
Meko denotes wife and children together. The Portuguese molher and filhos explicitly establish this collective family sense.

runs.text: Certa feição de dourar com folha dou-

lines.note: Mekki is a method of gilding with gold leaf. The word ouro is divided after dou- in the contracted phrase folha douro and continues on the next physical row.
Ro completes the gold-leaf definition. Mekki wo sasu is applying that gilding, directly translated as Dourar de folha; the long s forms are not f.
Mekkyaku means destruction. The following Mekkyaku su- begins the verbal example, completed by ru on the next row.
Ru completes suru, making “destroy,” as the Portuguese Deſtruir states. No period is supplied between ru and the gloss because none is securely visible.
Mekki mekki to is marked as an adverb and describes a particular creaking or cracking sound. The phonetic form is not the unrelated gilding noun just above.

runs.text: que faz a caſa quando treme com algum vento

lines.note: The sound is illustrated by a house shaking in wind. The adjective describing the wind continues on the next line.

runs.text: rijo, ou como quando quebra algum pao, &c.

lines.note: Rijo completes the strong-wind example, followed by a comparison with wood breaking. The next column adds another usage of the same reduplicated expression.
The construction work advances rapidly or visibly: this is another example of mekki mekki to. The first repetition prints mecqi, not provisional meeqi; michiga iqu is retained as the printed phrase.

runs.text: obra vai a olhos viſtos por diante.

lines.note: Completes the Portuguese sentence: the work goes forward before one’s eyes. This is a figurative-progress sense, not a further description of cracking timber.

runs.text: Diz ſe de hũa peßoa eſperta

lines.note: Mekuchi kawaki describes an alert or quick-witted person. The supplied NINJAL index independently lists Mecuchi cauaqi; the unfamiliar wording is therefore not silently changed to a more familiar Japanese expression.
Viva and sagaz complete the characterization as lively and shrewd. They belong to the same person introduced on the previous row.

runs.text: Hum preguinho de pao que tem mão

lines.note: Mekugi is a small wooden retaining peg. The Portuguese expression tem mão describes its holding or securing function, completed by the reference to the sword hilt.
The peg holds at the katana’s hilt. Catana is the sword-name occurring within the Portuguese explanation; the printed type is retained for optional whole-word review.
Mekugi ana is the hole through which that retaining peg is inserted. The printed space before ana is preserved rather than joining the compound.
Prego completes the definition of the peg-hole. This short continuation is not an independent entry or a displaced catchword.
Mekura denotes blindness or a blind person. The Portuguese vowel is e in Cego, not the provisional Cago.

runs.text: Balea femea: mais ſe vſa por,

lines.note: Mekujira is a female whale. The gloss says the word occurs more as a reading of a written term than in ordinary use; Yo- begins the roman Japanese word Yomi.
Mi completes Yomi, and Qeiguei is the term whose reading is being explained. The Portuguese prints pratica, not provisional pracica; both Japanese terms remain separate from the italic apparatus.
Mekurumeku concerns dizziness, explained by me no moo koto. The S. is an upright written-register label; the visually clear mǒ is retained rather than normalized to a modern verbal form.

runs.text: ença de andar a cabeça à roda, ou irſe o lume

lines.note: Ença completes Doença: the head spins, or the light of vision goes away. Both clauses describe dizziness or visual dimming.

runs.text: dos olhos. Não ſe vſa tanto em pratica co-

lines.note: Completes the reference to the eyes and begins the usage restriction: this is less a conversational word than a reading of a written expression.

Yomi and Qen vn are roman terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation. The printed initial Q and the internal space in Qen vn are preserved rather than regularized from the expected Japanese lexical identification.
Memaiqe is supplied as the current spoken word. It belongs inside the Portuguese sentence “the current word is,” rather than forming a separate headword here.
Medachi, medatsu, medatta here means a tree putting forth growth. The Portuguese brotar fixes the budding sense, not the modern prominent or conspicuous sense of medatsu.
New buds and leaves complete the description of the tree’s sprouting. Gomos is the botanical noun in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Folhas, ou gomos tenros das aruores

lines.note: The noun medachi denotes the tender leaves or buds themselves. It is separately entered after the verb’s principal forms.
The leaves or buds are those appearing when trees first begin to sprout. The small mark above the opening word is not taken as an abbreviation replacing the fully printed quando.
Mede, medzuru, medeta means taking delight or pleasure in something. Printed compra- continues as comprazerſe below; it is not an independent word.
Completes comprazerſe dalgũa couſa and introduces the peacock example. Cujacuuo fajimete means seeing a peacock for the first time in the sentence continued below.

The people who saw it were captivated by its beauty: miqeru fitoua and itçucuxiſani replace the malformed OCR. Fitoua is abraded but identifiable; the t after i in itçucuxiſani is nearly lost, so that letter remains a nonblocking contextual reconstruction rather than a fully clear impression.

runs.text: te qimouo qexi, aqire fatçurubacari nari.

lines.note: Te completes medete, followed by losing one’s composure and becoming utterly astonished. The phrase’s historical forms are retained rather than recast into modern Japanese.

runs.text: Os que virão a primeira vez o pauão recrea-

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the people’s first sight of the peacock. Recrea- begins the description of their delight; virão retains the historical printed ending.

runs.text: dos, & leuados de ſua fermoſura ficarão ato-

lines.note: They are delighted and carried away by its beauty, and become ato- across the line break. Fermoſura is the source’s spelling of beauty.
Nitos completes atonitos, astonished. Hikidemono ni medzuru then introduces a different application: being swayed by gifts.

runs.text: mouido de dadiuas, ou ſobornado de peitas.

lines.note: The Portuguese makes the inducement explicit: moved by gifts or bribed with peitas. This is the morally negative extension of taking pleasure in something.
Hana no iro ka ni medzuru means delighting in flowers’ color and fragrance. The printed separation iro cani is retained, and the translation continues below.
Seeing and smelling flowers and roses complete the illustration of delight. The two senses correspond to color and fragrance in the Japanese phrase.

runs.text: Couſa alegre, ou de bom ſucceßo.

lines.note: Medetai describes something joyful or fortunate. The print has ſucceßo, without the extra t in the provisional ſucceßto.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Palaura com que ſe dão as graças

lines.note: A second usage treats medetai as a formula of thanks or congratulation. Its Portuguese construction continues with para bens on the next row.
Completes the congratulatory usage, with the historical separated para bens. Dalgũa couſa states what the congratulations concern.
Medetasa is the abstract noun corresponding to medetai, joyfulness or felicity. Its separate indented physical line is preserved without adding a gloss.
Medetǒ gives the corresponding contracted adverbial or formulaic form. The clearly downward accent remains a caron; no explanatory words are supplied to the source text.

runs.text: O adeuinhar, ou conjeiturar com cere-

lines.note: Medo concerns divination or conjecture performed through ceremonies. The Portuguese cere- continues as ceremonias on the next row.

runs.text: monias ſuperſticioſas ſobre a vida, fortuna,

lines.note: The ceremonies concern a person’s life and fortune. The evaluative adjective ſuperſticioſas is the dictionary’s own characterization.
The list concludes with someone’s outcome or success. Medo wo toru begins an example of performing this kind of divination.

runs.text: Ver, ou cõjeiturar a vida, ou ſucceßo decada hũ

lines.note: The example is translated as discerning or conjecturing each person’s life or outcome. The abbreviated cõjeiturar and hũ are preserved without expansion.

runs.text: cõ estas ceremonias, & obſeruãdo certos põtos,

lines.note: The prediction uses ceremonies and observation of certain points. The tilde abbreviations cõ, obſeruãdo and põtos remain on their printed carriers.

runs.text: ou linhas judiciarias q̃ cõſiderão os Astrologos.

lines.note: The observed marks are divinatory lines considered by astrologers. The abbreviations q̃ and cõſiderão are retained, without adopting the gloss’s theory as a factual explanation.
Medori is a female bird. The gloss is generic ave femea, not a specific claim that only a domestic hen is intended.

runs.text: Meliùs, Memaje. O dar de olho.

lines.note: Mehajiki denotes signaling with the eye. Meliùs recommends Memaje as the preferable form; Memaje is a Japanese term embedded in the italic Portuguese apparatus.
Mehajiki wo suru means giving a sign with the eye. The visible opening paragraph sign was omitted by the draft and is restored before the Japanese example.
Mehitsuji is a female sheep, directly glossed Ouelha. The historical tç spelling is retained.
Mega is a female deer, described by both cerua and veado femea. This is another female-animal formation rather than the eye-plus-particle sequence of earlier examples.

runs.text: Pondo os olhos em algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: Megakete means directing one’s eyes or aim toward something. Vt introduces an example that continues on f313; the separate Mega catchword is page furniture, not an extra body row.
